![Scientists are busy trying to understand the black box of large language models (generated by DALL-E 3)](/images/ai-pause-what-is-it-and-why-should-busin-1.jpg)
*Scientists are busy trying to understand the black box of large language models (generated by DALL-E 3)*

Generative AI has taken the world by storm. Everyone from — businesses to municipal governments — are scrambling to implement “ChatGPT on their own data” at a pace that makes it hard to believe that ChatGPT will turn 11 months (months!) tomorrow. With [a recent study](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/how-generative-ai-can-boost-highly-skilled-workers-productivity) showing that AI can boost worker productivity by as much as 40%, the seems to be no reason to slow down. Yet, leading researchers, entrepreneurs, engineers and concerned citizens are advocating for just that — a pause to giant AI experiments. What does this mean for businesses? And why should they care?

## Understanding the AI (Scaling) Pause

The term ‘AI pause’ gained prominence from [an open letter drafted by the Future of Life Institute](https://futureoflife.org/open-letter/pause-giant-ai-experiments/). This letter, signed by more than 33,000 people including Elon Musk, Stuart Russell, Valerie Pisano, and yours truly, calls for a halt in large training runs of AI models. Specifically, it calls for pausing models requiring more computing power than GPT-4 (which cost a whopping $100M dollars to train [according to Sam Altman](https://www.wired.com/story/openai-ceo-sam-altman-the-age-of-giant-ai-models-is-already-over/)). To avoid confusion, I will call it the “AI Scaling Pause”, as I think this more succinctly captures what the letter calls for.

Here, I will briefly explain what I mean by “scaling” and why Large Language Models keep getting, well, larger. Basically, it’s about [*scaling laws*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)*;* the empirical observation that as language models get larger ([with correspondingly more data and computing power](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)), they get predictably better at predicting the next word (which, greatly simplified, is why they are useful).

Intuitively, this makes a pause sound even more counterproductive from a business perspective: why shouldn’t we want the models to get better? However, there are two crucial caveats: We don’t understand *why* the models get better and we don’t understand *what* they will learn.

## The Current Understanding Gap

When I say *we* don’t understand, I don’t just mean that *I* don’t understand. I mean that *no one*, not at leading academic institutions nor at the companies building these models has a good [*mechanistic* understanding](https://www.neelnanda.io/mechanistic-interpretability/glossary) of how large language models work. These models are insanely complicated: they have billions of non-linear parameters, are trained on colossal amounts of text, and are fine-tuned on ([relatively undiverse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.05453)) human feedback with [complex algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05862).

That is not to say that there is no progress. There is a lot of fascinating research on [how transformers learn](https://www.anthropic.com/index/decomposing-language-models-into-understandable-components), what distinguishes prompting from fine-tuning, how [sentiment is represented in language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15154), and much more. However, much of this research is conducted on smaller, more manageable models and toy problems. Being able to understand the models of today is an unsolved scientific problem that may be incredibly challenging.

The challenge of understanding large language models is similar to the difference between studying mice and humans in cognitive neuroscience. Fascinating findings on how mice solve problems don’t always work in humans (which is somewhat reassuring!). In the same way, understanding smaller language models doesn’t give us a complete picture of how larger ones function. Finding ways to scale up our knowledge from smaller models to larger ones is a big, unsolved problem.

This lack of understanding should be a red flag for business leaders considering implementing AI. While these models can assist in various tasks such as email proofreading, code writing, and data analysis, they can also lull us into a*nthropomorphism;* the tendency to interpret the thinking processes of LLMs as human-like — even though they are very different as illustrated in the below meme. Because their outputs are in human language it’s easy to attribute human thinking, which can lead to over-reliance.

![Shoggoth AI safety meme as described by the New York Times](/images/ai-pause-what-is-it-and-why-should-busin-2.jpg)
*Shoggoth AI safety meme as described by [the New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/05/30/technology/shoggoth-meme-ai.html)*

Overreliance has measurable consequences. [The same study](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/how-generative-ai-can-boost-highly-skilled-workers-productivity) that found an up to 40% increase in productivity, found a 25% *decrease* in productivity when the models were used outside of their capabilities. Here, the LLMs were still used as assistants. If the models were given more autonomously — i.e., being used to automate decisions for, say, hiring —the consequences could get much worse. We know from countless papers that AI is prone to encapsulate harmful stereotypes found in the training data. And without getting political I think most people can agree that we would like to shape the future in a better direction than the past — without having AI make those decisions for us!

## Risks and Opportunities

So, why are researchers calling for a pause? The concern is that as these models continue to get better at their tasks, they could also become riskier, especially since we don’t have a full grasp of their inner workings. The last thing we want is for these ‘black-box’ systems to cause unintended and unpredictable consequences in critical business operations (like doing risky financial transactions) or bad ethical decisions (like stopping hiring people of color).

However, a pause in scaling does not mean a halt in experimentation and adoption. In fact, businesses stand to benefit from a pause because it allows for better risk assessment and responsible deployment. Current models like the ones powering ChatGPT or open-source models like [zephyr](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceH4/zephyr-7b-beta), are powerful enough for a multitude of tasks that can benefit businesses today. There’s room to explore, understand limitations, and build robust systems without necessarily making them larger.

## There is no dilemma

Often, the discourse surrounding AI safety is painted as a battle between two opposing camps: the ‘alarmists’ who worry about AI risks and the ‘techno-optimists’ who are keen to deploy AI solutions as quickly as possible.

This perception of a divide often obscures the reality: there’s substantial agreement between those cautious about AI’s risks and those optimistic about its benefits. For instance, utilizing ChatGPT to convert rough drafts into polished emails is a widely accepted use that poses little danger. However, it’s equally important to recognize that we need a deeper understanding of both the risks and benefits these models offer before deploying them indiscriminately across all applications.

Advocating for an AI scaling pause is not the same as discouraging AI adoption. The pause will likely have zero effects on 99% of the AI implementations that businesses are considering. It doesn’t prevent companies from utilizing existing models or experimenting with new techniques like retrieval-augmented generation or fine-tuning — unless you plan on spending hundreds of millions of dollars on computing power!

## Conclusion

An AI scaling pause is not a roadblock but a necessary speed bump as we navigate the path of technological progress. It offers us time: time for researchers to understand these complex systems better, and time for businesses to experiment responsibly. Far from being an anti-progress stance, it’s a call for balanced and thoughtful advancement. In the grand scheme of things, businesses should not just be aware of the call for an AI safety pause; they should welcome it.
